question: What is a primary disadvantage of the oral drug administration route?

options.A: It is always more expensive than intravenous administration.
options.B: It has a slower onset of action compared to parenteral routes.
options.D: It is completely free of the first-pass effect.

explanation: Oral medications must pass through the digestive system and liver before entering the systemic circulation, which results in a slower onset of action compared to intravenous routes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: Which clinical assessment is critical before administering any oral medication to a patient?

options.B: Verifying an intact swallowing reflex and patent airway
options.C: Measuring the patient's daily fluid intake and output

explanation: A patient must have an intact swallowing reflex and patent airway to safely swallow oral medications and prevent aspiration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h1)

question: How many patient identifiers should a nurse use before administering medication?

options.A: One identifier, such as the room number
options.D: No identifiers are necessary if the nurse knows the patient

explanation: Nurses must always use at least two distinct patient identifiers, such as checking the ID band and asking for name and date of birth, to prevent medication errors. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h2)

question: What is the recommended patient position for safe oral medication administration?
explanation: Placing the patient in a High Fowler's position at a 90-degree angle facilitates safe swallowing and reduces the risk of aspiration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h2)

question: When should the nurse compare the medication label with the Medication Administration Record (MAR)?

options.A: Only after the medication has been swallowed
options.B: At least three times during retrieval, preparation, and administration
options.C: Only when the pharmacist delivers the drug
options.D: Once at the end of the shift

explanation: The safety check requires comparing the medication label to the MAR at least three times to catch discrepancies before the patient receives the drug. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h3)

question: What is the acceptable time window for administering most routine scheduled medications?

options.A: Within 2 hours before or after the scheduled time
options.B: Within 30 minutes before or after the scheduled time
options.D: Exactly on the dot with zero margin of error

explanation: Routine medications are generally administered within a 30-minute window before or after the scheduled time to maintain proper therapeutic blood levels. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h3)

question: How should a nurse accurately measure liquid medication in a medicine cup?

options.A: Hold the cup up to eye level and pour to the top rim
options.B: Place the cup on a flat surface and read the liquid level at the base of the meniscus at eye level
options.C: Estimate the volume using a standard household teaspoon
options.D: Measure from the highest peak of the liquid meniscus

explanation: Measuring liquid requires placing the cup on a flat surface and reading the base of the meniscus at eye level to ensure accurate dosage delivery. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which of the following medication types should never be crushed or chewed?

options.D: Soft gelatin capsules filled with oil

explanation: Enteric-coated and sustained-release tablets have special coatings designed to release medication slowly or protect the stomach; crushing them destroys this mechanism and can cause harm. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h4)

question: What must the nurse do immediately after handing the medication to the patient?

options.A: Leave the room to document immediately
options.B: Stay at the bedside and observe the patient swallow every medication
options.C: Place any remaining pills on the bedside table for later
options.D: Turn off the lights to let the patient rest

explanation: The nurse must remain at the bedside to ensure the patient actually swallows the medication and does not hoard or discard it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: What is the correct action if a patient drops a medication pill on the floor?

options.A: Wash it with water and administer it anyway
options.B: Discard the dropped pill according to policy and obtain a replacement
options.C: Put it back in the medication stock bottle
options.D: Ask the patient to pick it up and swallow it

explanation: Dropped medications are contaminated and must be discarded according to institutional policy, followed by obtaining a fresh replacement dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h5)

question: Which strategy is most effective when administering liquid medication to an uncooperative infant or young child?

options.A: Force the medication rapidly down the throat
options.B: Use an oral syringe to slowly place the medication into the side of the child's mouth
options.C: Mix the entire day's dose into a large bottle of milk
options.D: Inject the oral medication intramuscularly instead

explanation: Using an oral syringe to place the liquid into the side of the child's mouth helps prevent choking and ensures the child swallows the dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h6)

question: Why is geriatric medication administration particularly challenging?

options.A: Elderly patients metabolize drugs much faster than young adults
options.B: Polypharmacy, physiological changes, and conditions like dysphagia are common
options.C: Older adults never experience cognitive decline
options.D: Geriatric patients refuse all forms of liquid medication

explanation: Older adults frequently take multiple medications (polypharmacy), have altered pharmacokinetics due to aging, and may struggle with swallowing or cognitive issues. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h6)

question: When should the nurse document that a medication has been administered?

options.B: Promptly after the patient has taken the medication
options.C: At the end of the 8-hour shift
options.D: Only if the patient experiences an adverse reaction

explanation: Medications must always be documented promptly after administration to prevent duplicate dosing and ensure accurate medical records. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h7)

question: What action should a nurse take if a patient refuses a prescribed medication?

options.A: Force the patient to take the drug against their will
options.B: Hide the medication in the patient's food without telling them
options.C: Document the refusal along with the reason and notify the physician
options.D: Throw away the medication chart and ignore the refusal

explanation: Patients have the right to refuse medication; the nurse must document the refusal and reason, then inform the healthcare provider. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T14#GNS122_U1_T14_h7)
